question: If the order of checking learned from each verdict, would the same number of checks find more good companies than today's fixed ranking?

design.check: one check reveals one company's hidden label and costs 1
design.pairing: every policy sees the same subsample and tie-break order for a seed; differences are policy minus today-semantic, per seed
design.intervals: 95% percentile bootstrap, 2,000 resamples: over seeds within a pool; over pools and then seeds for the overall figures

policies.today-semantic: production today: semanticRelevance(brief, company text), checked from the top down; nothing learned
policies.today-lexical: production with no embedder: lexicalRelevance (word overlap with the segment's categories), top down; ties in seeded random order
policies.rocchio: after each batch the brief vector moves toward the mean of checked positives and away from checked negatives; companies are re-scored with production's formula
policies.cal-logreg: continuous active learning: L2 logistic regression on the embedding plus today's score, retrained after every batch, checks the highest-scored
policies.cal-uncertainty: the same model, but checks the company closest to even odds
policies.cal-logreg-egreedy: cal-logreg with a share of checks spent on a random unchecked company
policies.thompson: Bayesian linear model on a projection of the embedding plus today's score (prior mean: today's score); checks the best company under one posterior sample per check
policies.linucb: the same Bayesian model; checks the highest predicted score plus an uncertainty bonus
policies.knn-feedback: today's score plus mean cosine to the nearest checked positives minus mean cosine to the nearest checked negatives
policies.random: lower bound: a seeded random order
policies.oracle: upper bound: every good company first

tuning.rule: per learner, the grid setting with the most good companies after 100 checks, averaged over the development segments and seeds; the first value wins a tie

prefixDecision.rule: the mode with the higher mean average precision of today's ranking on the development segments; plain wins a tie

findings: Headline, with every brief in the buyers' own language (4 pools with English briefs, 3 Norwegian register pools with Norwegian briefs): after 25 / 50 / 100 / 200 checks today's fixed ranking has found 18.8 / 33.7 / 59.2 / 96.4 good companies and linucb, the learner picked on the development segments before any reported pool was run, has found 20.8 / 42.0 / 80.9 / 139.2 (the oracle: 25.0 / 50.0 / 98.2 / 179.9). Paired difference to today: +2.0 (95% interval -0.5 to +4.8) at 25; +8.3 (95% interval +2.5 to +15.3) at 50; +21.7 (95% interval +11.4 to +33.0) at 100; +42.8 (95% interval +31.5 to +53.6) at 200. The intervals resample pools and seeds. Pool by pool (intervals over seeds), linucb is ahead in 3 of 7 pools and behind in 1 at 25 checks, and ahead in 7 of 7 pools and behind in 0 at 100.

Best in hindsight under the same condition: cal-logreg has found 21.8 / 43.7 / 83.2 / 140.4 good companies after 25 / 50 / 100 / 200 checks. Paired difference to today: +3.0 (95% interval +0.6 to +5.9) at 25; +10.0 (95% interval +4.8 to +16.5) at 50; +24.0 (95% interval +14.4 to +34.6) at 100; +44.0 (95% interval +33.0 to +54.6) at 200. It was picked on these same pools, so its figures lean optimistic. At 100 checks cal-logreg minus linucb is +2.3 (95% interval +0.6 to +4.2).

Filling a shortlist of 25 under the same condition: today's ranking needs 28.8 checks in the median pool and 67.9 in the worst (brreg-coffee-tea); linucb needs 28.6 checks in the median pool and 45.9 in the worst (yc-devtools); cal-logreg needs 26.8 checks in the median pool and 41.3 in the worst (yc-devtools). Averaged over the pools today needs 40.1 checks and linucb 30.7, a difference of -9.4 (95% interval -20.8 to -0.2) checks; pool by pool linucb needs fewer checks in 4 of 7 and more in 2.

Where the gain at 100 checks comes from: on the 4 English-language pools (yc-devtools, yc-healthcare, yc-climate-energy and yc-logistics) linucb gains +15.4 (95% interval +5.5 to +29.9) over today and cal-logreg +19.4 (95% interval +8.8 to +34.4); on the 3 Norwegian pools with Norwegian briefs (brreg-coffee-tea, brreg-breweries and brreg-dental-bergen) linucb gains +30.1 (95% interval +20.0 to +47.7) and cal-logreg +30.2 (95% interval +20.0 to +47.9). Each of these two intervals rests on few pools.

The findings marked [First run] describe the first run, which gave all 7 pools an English brief (results.overall and results.perPool); the 4 English-language pools are the same in both. An English brief handicaps today's ranking on the 3 Norwegian pools: there it finds 11.5 / 16.6 / 25.0 good companies after 25 / 50 / 100 checks against 20.0 / 34.3 / 58.5 with a Norwegian brief, and on brreg-dental-bergen it needs 338 checks to fill the shortlist against 29. The first run therefore overstates what learning adds for a seller who writes in the buyers' language: linucb gains +34.7 good companies at 100 checks in the first run and +21.7 under the headline condition.

[First run] Starting point: across the 7 pools today's semantic ranking has a mean average precision of 0.337 (the word-overlap fallback: 0.271; a random order would score about the prevalence, 0.084). Of its first 25 checks 15.2 are good on average, from 8.7 on brreg-breweries to 23.1 on yc-climate-energy.

[First run] Same checks, more good companies: after 25 / 50 / 100 / 200 checks today's fixed ranking has found 15.2 / 26.1 / 44.8 / 75.4 good companies and the best learner, cal-logreg, has found 19.4 / 40.8 / 80.8 / 139.1 (the oracle: 25.0 / 50.0 / 98.2 / 179.9). Paired difference to today: +4.2 (95% interval +1.7 to +6.5) at 25; +14.7 (95% interval +7.7 to +21.9) at 50; +36.0 (95% interval +19.6 to +52.8) at 100; +63.7 (95% interval +33.0 to +102.7) at 200. The intervals resample pools and seeds. Pool by pool (intervals over seeds), cal-logreg is ahead in 6 of 7 pools at 25 checks and behind in 0; ahead in 7 at 100 and behind in 0.

[First run] Filling a shortlist of 25: today's ranking needs 90.9 checks on average (27 to 338 by pool, median pool 52) and cal-logreg 32.0 (27 to 41, median 29), a difference of -58.9 (95% interval -141.7 to -9.4) checks. The mean leans on the slowest pool; pool by pool cal-logreg needs fewer checks in 6 of 7 and more in 0. Runs that did not fill the shortlist within 500 checks count as 500 (today filled it in 100% of runs, cal-logreg in 100%).

[First run] All learners at 100 checks, as good companies gained over today's ranking: cal-logreg +36.0 (+19.6 to +52.8); linucb +34.7 (+16.1 to +54.1); knn-feedback +34.1 (+16.4 to +53.2); cal-logreg-egreedy +30.4 (+13.2 to +47.2); cal-uncertainty +23.6 (+6.4 to +41.6); rocchio +17.9 (+5.0 to +35.8); thompson +14.5 (+2.6 to +27.1). At 25 checks: cal-logreg +4.2; linucb +3.9; knn-feedback +5.3; cal-logreg-egreedy +2.4; cal-uncertainty +3.1; rocchio +3.9; thompson -2.1.

[First run] The best learner is not clearly best: at 100 checks cal-logreg minus linucb is +1.3 (95% interval -1.6 to +4.0), minus knn-feedback is +1.9 (95% interval -2.2 to +6.1). linucb and knn-feedback cannot be told apart from cal-logreg on these pools; the remaining learners are behind it.

[First run] Where today's ranking is already near the oracle (at least 20 good in today's first 25 checks: yc-healthcare with 22.6 and yc-climate-energy with 23.1), learning adds little early and does no harm: cal-logreg versus today after 25 / 50 / 100 checks is yc-healthcare -0.1 / +1.1 / +6.7; yc-climate-energy +0.5 / +5.4 / +12.9. The gain comes later, once today's ranking has used up its obvious matches.

[First run] Where today's ranking leaves room (between 5 and 20 good in today's first 25 checks: yc-devtools with 11.3, yc-logistics with 14.8, brreg-coffee-tea with 14.4, brreg-breweries with 8.7 and brreg-dental-bergen with 11.6), learning pays from the first batches: cal-logreg versus today after 25 / 50 / 100 checks is yc-devtools +1.6 / +7.2 / +16.5; yc-logistics +7.4 / +15.8 / +41.5; brreg-coffee-tea +8.5 / +29.1 / +47.1; brreg-breweries +6.9 / +17.6 / +54.3; brreg-dental-bergen +4.5 / +26.6 / +73.2.

[First run] No pool starts almost empty (5 or fewer good in today's first 25 checks); the lowest is brreg-breweries with 8.7 (with every brief in the buyers' language, yc-devtools with 11.3). So this experiment does not show how a learner fares when the first batches bring back no positive at all.

[First run] Today's ranking can run dry: on brreg-dental-bergen it finds 11.6 good companies in its first 25 checks and 2.9 in the next 75, no better than a random order (9.2). cal-logreg finds 87.5 by 100 checks there and fills the shortlist in 36 checks instead of 338. With the Norwegian brief today's ranking does not run dry there: 22.9 good companies in its first 25 checks and 52.4 in the next 75.

[First run] The word-overlap fallback finds 14.6 / 25.0 / 41.2 good companies after 25 / 50 / 100 checks, -3.6 (95% interval -11.8 to +6.8) against the semantic ranking at 100. It is ahead on yc-logistics and brreg-dental-bergen and behind on yc-devtools, yc-healthcare, yc-climate-energy, brreg-coffee-tea and brreg-breweries.

[First run] Exploring costs checks at these budgets: against cal-logreg's 80.8 good companies after 100 checks, spending 10% of checks at random finds 75.3, checking the most uncertain company finds 68.4 and Thompson sampling finds 59.3 (today: 44.8).

[First run] The development segments alone, before any reported pool was run, would have picked linucb, not cal-logreg. On the reported pools linucb gains +3.9 (95% interval +0.8 to +6.7) at 25 checks, +14.3 (95% interval +5.1 to +23.4) at 50 and +34.7 (95% interval +16.1 to +54.1) at 100, and needs 32.4 checks for the shortlist. Those are the figures free of hindsight; the ones for cal-logreg are a best-of-7 picked on these same pools and lean optimistic.

[First run] Batch size 1 instead of 5: cal-logreg finds 20.1 / 41.6 / 81.7 good companies after 25 / 50 / 100 checks (batches of 5: 19.4 / 40.8 / 80.8); its gain over today at 100 checks is +36.9 (95% interval +20.0 to +54.1).

[First run] Batch size 10 instead of 5: cal-logreg finds 18.8 / 39.7 / 80.1 good companies after 25 / 50 / 100 checks (batches of 5: 19.4 / 40.8 / 80.8); its gain over today at 100 checks is +35.3 (95% interval +19.7 to +50.7).

Norwegian briefs on the 3 register pools: today's ranking finds 20.0 / 34.3 / 58.5 good companies after 25 / 50 / 100 checks with a Norwegian brief against 11.5 / 16.6 / 25.0 with the English one; cal-logreg finds 23.9 / 47.8 / 88.7 against 18.1 / 41.0 / 83.2. With the Norwegian brief cal-logreg's gain over today at 100 checks is +30.2 (95% interval +20.0 to +47.9): a brief in the companies' own language lifts today's ranking and narrows the gap, and the learner still adds to it. Of the good companies, production's relevance gate keeps 100% on brreg-coffee-tea, 99% on brreg-breweries and 100% on brreg-dental-bergen with the Norwegian brief, against 93% on brreg-coffee-tea, 60% on brreg-breweries and 11% on brreg-dental-bergen with the English one.

Task prefixes: on the development segments today's ranking has a mean average precision of 0.3883 without nomic-embed-text's search_query/search_document prefixes and 0.3659 with them, so every policy uses the plain vectors. On the reported pools the plain vectors give today's ranking the higher average precision in 6 of 7 (the other way round on brreg-dental-bergen, 0.124 against 0.139).

Production drops companies whose relevance is not above zero before any check. In the first run, with English briefs for all pools, that gate keeps 61% of a pool on average and 79% of its good companies (lowest: 11% on brreg-dental-bergen). With Norwegian briefs it keeps, of the good companies, 100% on brreg-coffee-tea, 99% on brreg-breweries and 100% on brreg-dental-bergen; over the 7 pools with every brief in the buyers' language that makes 86% of a pool on average and 98% of its good companies. The simulation ignores the gate, so a learner here may reach good companies that production never checks.
limits: Labels are directory tags and register codes, not buying decisions: a company can be a real prospect without the tag, and a register code can disagree with what the company's text says. Every policy is scored against the same labels.

These labels follow from what a company's text is about (its industry, its registered activity), which is the kind of verdict that is easiest to learn from embeddings. A real verdict also turns on things the text does not say (size, timing, an existing supplier), so expect smaller gains in production than here.
A check reveals the true label. In production the verdict comes from a chat model and then a person, both of which are sometimes wrong; no label noise is simulated.

The embedding model is the local nomic-embed-text, weaker than a paid model, most of all on Norwegian text read against an English brief. A stronger model would lift today's ranking and leave the learners less to add.
The briefs carry no seller profile and no partner kind, which production appends; a real brief is longer and drifts further from the buyers' own words.

Hyper-parameters were picked on two other segments of the Y Combinator directory. The four reported YC segments share that pool's companies (not its labels); the three register pools were never seen before the reported run.
Seven pools from two sources. The overall intervals resample pools and seeds, but seven pools cannot stand for every segment a customer will write.
Runs that did not fill the shortlist within 500 checks count as 500, which understates how much slower they are.
The simulation ignores production's relevance-above-zero gate and counts cost in checks only; a learner's own computation (a small model refit per batch) is not counted.
The batch-size runs cover 6 policies: the two variants of cal-logreg and the policies a batch size cannot change are left out.

The headline condition (every brief in the buyers' language) was chosen after the first run was reviewed. Its Norwegian-brief runs were planned as a sensitivity check, their briefs were written before any policy ran, and nothing was re-tuned for it; of the two conditions it is the less favourable one for the learners. The batch-size runs exist for the first run only.
